context:
FAQ: Entry from Ukraine and residence in Germany
Information from the Federal Foreign Office and the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees
Here you will find the latest information and situation reports from the Federal ForeignOffice and the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees.
Entry rules and visa requirements can also be found on the pages.
We have included some important questions and answers here:
I am in Germany without a visa.
What options do I have now?
They do not need a visa or residence permit to stay in Germany legally for up to 90 days from the date they enter.
During the 90 days in which you can stay in Germany legally without a visa, you can decide whether you would like to stay in Germany longer.
If you decide to stay longer, you have the following options:
Within 90 days of entering Germany for the first time, you can apply for a temporary residence permit under section 24 of the Residence Act (Aufenthaltsgesetz, AufenthG).
Section 24 deals specifically with the situation of refugees from the war in Ukraine based on the relevant EU decision.
You can find out here who is eligible for a temporary residence permit under section 24 of the Residence Act, and you can find out more about the procedure here.
Within 90 days of entering Germany for the first time, you can apply for a temporary residence permit for a different purpose, such as to study or work in Germany.
This may be more advantageous for you.
You can make an appointment with the relevant government authorities to ask them for advice.
Or you can find out more by visiting the website www.make-it-in-germany.com.
Or you can apply for asylum.
However, we do not recommend this option, because it comes with some disadvantages: your right to take up employment would be subject to restrictions, and you would have to live in an initial reception centre.
What happens after I enter the country?
Where can I register in Germany and where do I get accommodation and food?
The procedure is divided into four successive steps: First registration and (in the case of benefit recipients) distribution to a place of residence, as well as registration of the residential address at the destination and application for a residence title.
You can find further information here.
Can I work in Germany with a residence permit for temporary protection?
Yes, you can.
However, gainful employment must first be permitted by the foreigners authority.
When the residence permit is issued, the foreigners authority will already enter in the residence title that gainful employment is permitted, even if no concrete job is in prospect yet.
This means that no further work permit from another authority is required.
The foreigners authorities will issue so-called probationary certificates when an application is submitted.
These bypass the residence law until the actual residence title can be issued and granted.
The foreigners authority will also enter "gainful employment permitted" in the probationary certificate.
Even with this probationary certificate, it is therefore possible to work in Germany on a self-employed basis or as an employee.
Special professional access requirements (such as a licence to practise medicine or a permit for a trade requiring a licence) naturally apply to temporarily protected persons just like to everyone else.
But the procedures for the recognition of foreign professional qualifications are also open to those affected, just like everyone else.
Persons with a residence permit for temporary protection in Germany are also eligible for advice and placement services in accordance with Social Code III (SGB III) through the employment agencies.
Should Ukrainian nationals have to apply for asylum?
No, that is not necessary.
The required protection will be granted in another, faster procedure.
Ukrainian nationals are therefore advised not to apply for asylum.
However, the right to apply for asylum at a later stage continues regardless.
As a result of the Decision to admit war refugees pursuant to Article 5 para.
Granting of residence for temporary protection) will be granted with immediate effect to the group of persons covered upon application.
Registration upon entry does not constitute an asylum application.
The implementation of an asylum procedure requires an application for asylum to be filed at the competent branch office of the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees.
For these reasons, filing an asylum application is not required to secure a right of residence or to claim social benefits.

The Federal Ministry of the Interior and Home Affairs offers a digital information service in German, English, Russian, and Ukrainian.
Here you can find all official information about residence and life in Germany.

Transfer of costs to the Job Centre
Transfer of costs to the Job Centre
If you are unemployed and receive benefits from the job centre, the job centre pays the rent.
However, only if you are in need of assistance and the rent is reasonable (not too high).
Each job centre sets its own rent ceiling, which can sometimes even vary within the same area of responsibility (e.g. Jobcenter Augsburg-Land).
Rent upper limit means: The Job Centre sets a maximum amount for the rent.
If your rent is more expensive, you have to pay the rest yourself.
The tables for the rent ceilings of the individual authorities can be found here:
Job Centre Augsburg City
Jobcenter Augsburg Land
What do you need to know?
Important: If you have found a flat and the rent is paid by the Job Centre, you must not sign the tenancy agreement straight away.
It is essential that the Job Centre checks and approves the adequacy of the accommodation costs prior to conclusion.
This is possible during regular opening hours and without an appointment.
The Jobcenter's decision on whether the costs are fair and whether it will pay the deposit will be given to you straight away in writing.
This is called a "rental confirmation".
It is important that a tenancy agreement or at least a rental offer with all minimum information about the flat is already available.
It is important to note that the tenancy agreement must already be signed by the landlord, but not by the tenant.
The following points must be included in the rental contract:
Name and address of the landlord
Address of the rental property
Living space in m²
Number of rooms
Amount of the net cold rent
Amount of operating costs
Amount of heating costs
Total rent
Amount of the deposit
Deposit
The Job Centre can grant the deposit on a loan basis upon application.
On a loan basis means: You get the money and have to pay it back.
As a rule, this is unproblematic and is granted for reasonable accommodation costs.
The deposit is usually paid directly to the landlord by the Job Centre.
The repayment of the loan to the Job Centre is automatically deducted from the monthly standard benefits (normally max.
ten percentof this) and retained.
Initial equipment
If you receive benefits from the Job Centre, you have the possibility to apply for initial equipment for furniture and furnishings.
You will be paid a lump sum according to the number of people, the size of the flat and the equipment required.
The initial equipment includes furniture, curtains, mattresses, cooking utensils, crockery and, if not available in the flat, a cooker, sink, refrigerator and washing machine.
It is important that the application is made before the furniture is purchased.
You can find a list with an overview of where you can buy cheap and used furniture "here.
Caution: It may take a while before the money is paid out!
In addition, the Jobcenter has (and uses) a right to inspect the flat to check what is needed for the initial outfitting.
If it is found that, for example, furniture is already in place, and you cannot prove (in writing!) that it has been lent to you (e.g. an emergency bed from SKM), you will no longer be entitled to a Starter Kit for those items.
Info for refugees
When you move out of accommodation, you are not allowed to take the furniture of the accommodation with you.
That's why you need new furniture.
You can apply to the Job Centre for initial equipment.

Freely selectable gender identity / LGBTQIA+
Gender diversity
Sexual orientation is a central aspect of one's personality.
In Germany, every person is allowed to choose their own sexual identity.
Everyone is free to decide who they are with and who they love.
And every person is free to live out their own sexual orientation.
Because this is an important right, it is enshrined in law (General Equal Treatment Act).
In Germany, a great deal of effort is being made to break down rigid role models and open up the view to all ways of life.
A lot has therefore happened in recent years:
Regardless of whether a gender reassignment from male to female or from female to male has taken place or is planned.
What does LGBTQIA+ or LGBT mean?
LGBTQIA+ or LGBT are abbreviations from the English language.
In German, the abbreviation LSBTTIQ is often used, which stands for the following terms:
L=lesbian - S=gay - B=bisexual - T=transgender - T=transsexual - I=intersexual - Q=queer.
Lesbians are women who love other women.
Gays are men who love other men.
Bisexuals fall in love with people, regardless of gender.
Transgender people are women who were born in a male body or men who were born in a female body.
Like transgender people, transsexuals are also born in the "wrong body" and change their appearance through hormones and operations.
Intersex people have both male and female genitals.
People with asexual orientation have little or no interest in sexual activity.
Queer stands for everything that deviates from traditional gender roles and partner models.
The "+" in LGBTQIA+ means that there are even more sexual or gender identities.
Support
You will also find acceptance and support in the district of Augsburg.
There are organisations that look after the LGBTIQ* scene.
In general, this is about
Equal rights and equal treatment
Fighting discrimination and misanthropy
Educating the LGBTIQ* scene
Contact points

More information at: https://comingout.de/
More information at: https://gladt.de/

Recommendation of combination vaccinations by the STIKO
Currently, the Standing Commission on Vaccination (STIKO) recommends the following combination vaccinations for children up to the age of 12:
1. 6-way combination vaccine against diphtheria, tetanus (lockjaw), polio, pertussis, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), hepatitis B:
Other vaccine combinations are also possible, for example without Hib and/or hepatitis B.
The 2+1 vaccination schedule is intended for this combination vaccination.
The 1. Vaccination should be given at the age of 2 months (from the 8th week of pregnancy).
Week of life).
The 2. The first vaccination should be scheduled eight weeks later (at the age of 4 months).
Dose another six months later, at the age of 11 months.
At the age of five to six years, the vaccination protection should be refreshed by a new vaccination.
A second course should be taken against diphtheria, polio and whooping cough.
Refresher training should take place between the ages of 9 and 17.
Afterwards, the vaccination protection can be renewed every ten years.
Information on the individual diseases
Diphtheria
Diphtheria is a bacterial infectious disease that can affect the mucous membranes of the throat and the skin.
Tetanus (lockjaw)
The tetanus bacterium often hides in the soil.
Even small wounds or bites from splinters and thorns are enough for the bacterium to enter the body.
Poliomyelitis (Polio)
Ca.
95% of those infected do not notice their infection.
About 5% have fever, sore throat and headache.
Infected persons suffer permanent, flaccid paralysis of the arm or leg muscles, in the worst case paralysis of the speech, swallowing or breathing muscles.
Whooping cough (pertussis)
The disease is characterised by flu-like symptoms.
These last for about two weeks.
In the following four to six weeks, the main symptoms are agonising coughing fits that can lead to vomiting.
Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib)
The rather unknown disease "Hib" can be severe, especially for infants and young children.
Possible consequences are meningitis and epiglottitis.
Hepatitis B
In the case of hepatitis B, a risk of contracting the disease is relatively low for infants without a family history of risk (i.e.: already known previous illnesses of other family members).
Nevertheless, the STIKO recommends vaccination, especially since there is a high risk of chronic forms of progression after an illness.
Chronic means that the disease develops slowly and lasts for a long time.
2. Combination vaccine against mumps, measles rubella (MMR) and, if applicable, chickenpox (MMRV):
With this vaccine combination, the 1. Vaccination recommended for children from the age of 11 to 14 months.
The 2. Vaccination can be given after a minimum interval of four weeks, but at the latest at an age of 15 to 23 months.
Information on the individual diseases
Mumps
Mumps is characterised by inflammation and consequently swelling of the parotid glands.
Ca.
1/3 of sick infants do not develop any signs of the disease themselves, but are contagious to other people.
Rubella
Rubella has particularly serious consequences for pregnant women.
Infection can harm the woman's unborn child during the first four months of pregnancy.
A high number of vaccinated persons can prevent a widespread spread.
That is why the vaccination recommendation is not only aimed at girls and women who want to have children.
Chickenpox (varicella)
Chickenpox is extremely easy to transmit, as almost every contact with an infected person leads to infection.
The consequences of chickenpox are fever and exhaustion in the first few days.
Later, there is a skin rash with blisters on the face, body and arms and legs.
Mucous membranes and the hairy scalp can also be affected by the rash.

context:
Online shopping
More and more people are shopping online.
There are a few things to bear in mind.
Remember:
Online shopping does not only have positive effects.
Packaging material and returns are a burden on the environment.
And local shops can't keep up with the competition on the internet either.
That's why many shops are closing.
Local shops are empty.
It is therefore worth considering what you order online or buy locally.
What should I look out for when shopping online?
Reputable online shop or fake shop?
Do you want to order something online?
Then you should find out about the online shop beforehand.
Because not all platforms are reputable.
So-called fake shops offer cheap goods that you don't receive after payment or that you receive in poor condition.
How can I recognise a dubious online retailer?
Conspicuously low price
The goods in the online shop are remarkably cheap?
This is not always a sign of a fake shop.
But you should take a closer look.
Conspicuous Internet address
A well-known website suddenly shows inconsistencies?
The domain extension has been extended (e.g. instead of ".de" it reads: ".de.com")?
The Internet address contains the keyword "plants", but shoes are being sold?
Then these are signs of a fake shop.
No legal notice:
Every online shop in the EU must have an imprint.
If the legal notice is missing, it is a sign of a dubious online shop.
However, scammers know this too.
Therefore, make sure that the legal notice includes the following: Address, representative, e-mail address, reference to the commercial register.
If these criteria are met, there is a high probability that it is a reputable shop.
Missing terms and conditions (general terms and conditions) and cancellation conditions
GTCs are pre-formulated contractual terms and conditions.
They are therefore rules that apply to every purchase from this online shop.
If you don't find any terms and conditions on the site, you should be careful with this online shop.
A reputable online shop will provide information about the cancellation conditions.
You have a right of cancellation for every purchase.
Unsafe payment methods
Normally the rule is: first the goods, then the payment.
However, many shops also offer prepayment.
Prepayment means that you transfer the money before the goods are dispatched.
Many payment methods are offered?
But in the last step you can only select "prepayment" as the payment method?
Then be careful!
False quality seals
Many fake shops use quality seals to gain the trust of potential customers.
Do you see a quality seal on an online shop?
Then click on it.
If the quality seal is not linked to the corresponding website, then it is probably a fake.
Missing or only positive customer reviews
Customer reviews on the online shop's website are not always meaningful.
Often only positive reviews are published.
Bad reviews are deleted.
However, you can also search for customer reviews on other platforms.
No encrypted connection
Make sure that the online shop has an encrypted connection.
Especially if you have to enter your data or bank details.
Insufficient product descriptions
Does the product description match the goods or services on offer?
If not, it could be a fake shop.
Defects in the offer
Before making a purchase, you should be informed about delivery times and shipping costs.
Be careful if this is not the case.
Lack of contact options
Avoid online shops that only offer an email address or a paid telephone number as a contact option.
You can easily check whether an online shop is reputable with the Fake Shop Finder from the consumer advice centre: Fake Shop Finder.
Tips for safe online shopping
Be careful when entering your details.
Of course, the online shop needs your name and address for delivery.
But sometimes other information is also requested.
Think about whether you really want to provide them.
Choose online shops carefully.
Pay attention to the criteria listed above.
Compare the prices with offers in the shop.
Not everything is cheaper on the internet.
Pay attention to the total price: Is the price shown really the final purchase price (including taxes, customs duties and shipping costs)?
Contact customer service if you are unsure about something.
Read the experiences and reviews of other customers.
Check again before you place the order: Which products are in your shopping basket?
What are the delivery costs?
Are there any additional taxes if the product comes from outside the EU?
Print out your order or purchase contract, the product description and the terms and conditions and cancellation policy or save them on your computer.
This way, the online retailer cannot change anything afterwards.
You can find more information on safe online shopping in German and Englishhere (including an explanatory video in German).

Dual apprenticeship
How does a dual apprenticeship work?
Candidates learn the theory at a vocational school (1 to 2 days per week) and the practical part at a company (3 to 4 days per week).
The training lasts two to three and a half years, depending on the profession.
Candidates receive a salary (just how much a person earns depends on the industry, company and year of the apprenticeship).
There are roughly 330 professions for which a candidate can undertake a dual apprenticeship.
Just how a dual apprenticeship works is explained in information films provided by the Bundesinstitut für Berufsbildung (Federal Institute for Vocational Education and Training) in 10 languages (Arabic, Chinese, German, English, Farsi, French, Italian, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish).
How do I find an apprenticeship place?
If you want to complete a dual training programme, you first have to find a training place.
You are applying for a training place at a company (enterprise, firm, institution).
"training place" means: You have a job in a company,in whichyou learn the practical work for the profession.
Only then comes the registration for the vocational school.
The company takes care of the registration.
The following online job exchanges will help you find an apprenticeship:
Job exchange of the employment agency www.jobboerse.arbeitsagentur.de
IHK apprenticeship exchange www.ihk-lehrstellenboerse.de
HWK apprenticeship exchange: www.hwk-schaben.de/lehrstellenb örse
Azubiyo apprenticeship exchange www.azubiyo.de/ausbildung
Training market www.ausbildungsmarkt.de
AUBI-Plus www.aubi-plus.de
Apprenticeship radar www.lehrstellen-radar.de
In addition to thesetrainee platforms, there arealso other optionsavailable online.
You can also use these.
You will also find training places
through the "AzubiWelt" app of the Federal Employment Agency (www.arbeitsagentur.de/azubiwelt)
in newspapers,
on company websites,
through unsolicited applications.
Which vocational school should I attend?
In most cases, vocational schools have specialised in what they offer.
In the district of Augsburg there are, for example, two subject areas at the vocational school Staatliches Berufliches Schulzentrum Neusäß: Business and Administration (office, industry, retail, wholesale) and Agricultural Economics (agriculture, landscaping, floristry).
If you want to do dual training in a different field, you will attend a different vocational school.
Who can help me to look for an apprenticeship?
There are numerous businesses which are on the lookout for candidates who wish to do an apprenticeship.
The following pages will help you with your search:
www.jobboerse.arbeitsagentur.de
www.ihk-lehrstellenboerse.de
www.hwk-schwaben.de/lehrstellenboerse
In many countries, the concept of a dual apprenticeship does not exist.
This means that many people arriving in Germany from abroad find it difficult to understand the principle of the German dual apprenticeship.
The KAUSA service point helps with information and provides intensive support in the search for an apprenticeship, with applications and with all questions during the apprenticeship:
KAUSA Service Point
info@aau-augsburg.de
Good to know: Many businesses put a lot of effort into finding apprentices early on, meaning that apprenticeship places are often fully subscribed and occupied a year in advance.

Rental contract (Mietvertrag) and security deposit (Kaution)
Rental contract
The amount of rent you pay is agreed in the rental contract.
If the tenant signs the contract, he also agrees to the rental payment.
The rent consists of the base rent, additional costs (refuse collection, operating costs) andheating costs.
The contract stipulates when the rent will be paid.
If the rent is increasingly not paid on time, this can leadto terminationof the lease contract.
You have to read the lease carefully.
If you don't understand everything, ask someone who can help you.
The lease contract is very important.
Once the contract is signed, it cannot be cancelled so quickly!
The following points must be included in the rental contract:
Name and address of the landlord
Address of the rental property
Living space in m²
Number of rooms
Amount of the net cold rent
Amount of operating costs
Amount of heating costs
Total rent
Amount of the deposit
If you agree with what is written in the lease, then sign the contract.
Deposit
The deposit is security for the landlord.
The amount of the deposit is a maximum ofthree cold rents.
If you move out of the flat and leave no damage behind, you will get the money back.

Permanent residence
What residence titles are there for permanent residence?
Settlement permit according to § 9 of the Residence Act
With a settlement permit, you can live and work in Germany.
Without time and place restrictions.
Prerequisites are, for example
Legal residence in Germany for at least 5 years (previous periods of study and training are counted at 50%)
Valid residence permit that was not issued for a temporary purpose (studies) or for humanitarian reasons
Proof of secure means of subsistence
Proof of secure accommodation
Proof of sufficient pension provision (at least 60 months of compulsory or voluntary contributions to statutory pension insurance in Germany)
Sufficient German language skills and basic knowledge of the legal and social order and living conditions in Germany - usually proven by
successful participation in an integration course
or
certificates and proof of study relating to vocational training completed in Germany
or
other language certificates
In individual cases, you may need additional documents.
You can find more information on the requirements here.
Permanent residence - EU
Permanent residence - EU is an unlimited residence title.
It offers the same rights as the settlement permit.
With this permit, you can live and work in Germany.
Without any time or place restrictions.
You can also live, work or study in other EU countries.
Exceptions are Ireland and Denmark.
Special regulations apply for individual countries.
You can find information on the requirements here.
Which residence permit is right for you?
That depends on your individual circumstances.
The
Immigration Office will be happy to advise you.
Keywords: residence title, permanent residence, settlement permit

Level B1 – for intermediates
Complete B1 course: "Nico's Way"
In this free and comprehensive course you will learn German at B1 level in 18 chapters.
Each chapter begins with a short video - structured in the style of a telenovela - on the basis of which you work through exercises and thus learn the German language step by step with Nico, the protagonist of the telenovela.
For each chapter there are explanations of the grammar, vocabulary lists, regional information and manuscripts for the video.
The website can be set to 9 different languages, including English, Arabic, Russian, Polish and more.
Complete B1 course with tutor
In this free course you will learn German at B1 level in 12 lessons with videos, audios, pictures and matching tasks.
In the learning portal you will find a vocabulary trainer and phrase trainer for each lesson, so that you can practise new vocabulary.
In addition, a tutor supports you online, who answers questions or corrects texts.
The portal can be set to 19 different languages, including English, Arabic, Turkish, Albanian, Serbian, Polish and many more.
Telenovela: "Jojo seeks happiness"
In three seasons of the telenovela you will learn more about the life of Jojo, a Brazilian who came to Germany, and her friends in Cologne.
Each episode of "Jojo sucht das Glück" is accompanied by interactive exercises and vocabulary aids for learning German.
B1 - German on the Job
With this free course you can practise German for your job.
You can choose from the following occupational areas: Gastronomy, systems engineering, building cleaning, nursing, retail.
For each occupational field, there are seven learning units with videos and subsequent tasks, with which you will mainly learn the vocabulary as well as the idioms and typical phrases used in the respective industry.
Learn German on the Deutsche Welle website
On the Deutsche Welle website you can find a wide variety of offers for learning German.
You can listen to news spoken more slowly for learners, you can find out how Germans live in the Germany Lab, you can meet other learners in the online community, watch videos on various topics, practise your listening comprehension, read up on grammar questions and, above all, do lots of exercises.
The site is available in 30 languages, including English, Arabic, Bosnian, Greek, Polish and many more.
German forum and online community
If you want to join a Whatsapp learning group, chat in German with learners from all over the world or look for a learning partner, you'll find what you're looking for in the online community on the Goethe-Institut site.
You will also find various German exercises at all levels, including B1.

Towns, markets and municipalities in the district
The district of Augsburg comprises 46 towns, markets and municipalities.
The district covers a large area.
From the northernmost municipality to the southernmost municipality it takes a good 45 minutes by car.
Here you can find a map of the district with all the towns, markets and municipalities.
Town, market or municipality?
Or a municipality after all?
It is not easy for many people to distinguish between these terms.
We would like to briefly explain them to you:
"Kommune" is a generic term for districts, towns, markets and municipalities.
"Municipality" is a generic term for towns and markets (not for rural districts, as rural districts are made up of municipalities).
"Towns" are municipalities with more than 5,000 inhabitants.
They also fulfil a central function for the surrounding municipalities due to their location.
"Markets" are municipalities with a historical or formally granted market right.
The market right certifies the importance of the municipality for the neighbouring municipalities.
For example, in terms of location, size or offer (e.g. many shops).
The market is an intermediate stage between a municipality and a town.
The term "market" is a speciality for Bavaria.
There are no markets in most German federal states.

If you need medication, you will get a prescription from your doctor.
You can get your medication with this prescription at any pharmacy.
Even with a prescription, not all medicines are free.
Therefore, ask your doctor about it.
If you don't have a prescription, you always have to pay for the medication.
Some medicines, such as antibiotics, require a prescription.
That means you can't buy them without a prescription.

Pharmacies are usually open from Monday to Saturday.

If you need medication urgently at night or at the weekend, you will find a sign at every pharmacy with the name and address of the pharmacy that is open for emergency service.

context:
Current account
The current account
With a current account, you can make payments and receive money.
Your money is always available in your current account.
With a current account you can:
Make bank transfers,
receive cashless payments (payments from public authorities (social benefits) are often made cashless, i.e. transferred to a personal current account),
set up standing orders,
participate in direct debits,
cashing cheques,
make cashless payments with the EC/Maestro card,
withdraw cash at bank counters or ATMs and
print out your account statements.
Important: You need enough money in your account for all withdrawals and payments.
Tip: A current account usually costs money.
The costs vary from bank to bank.
You also get different services depending on the bank.
Therefore, find out about the different conditions at the banks.
Opening an account and using the account
What do you need to look out for in a bank account?
And what do you need to open a bank account?
You can read about this at the consumer advice centre in two languages(German, Russian): www.verbraucherzentrale.de (search term: "multilingual information").
There you will also find explanatory videos on the topic in German, English, Arabic and Dari.
Important information
After opening the account, you will receive an EC card with a four-digit PIN code.
Sign the back of the EC card.
Memorise the PIN code.
You will need the PIN code for cashless payments and for withdrawing money from ATMs.
Make sure you keep your card and PIN code separate!
For cash withdrawals, it is best to use an ATM from your bank.
Then the withdrawal costs nothing.
You must enter the PIN code carefully at the ATM.
You only have three attempts.
After that, the debit card will be cancelled and blocked.
In this case, you must ask your bank about further steps.
In many supermarkets you can withdraw money from a certain purchase value.
Sometimes an EC card is lost or stolen.
If this happens, you should block your debit card immediately.
Use this telephone number: 116 116 (for all debit cards, 24 hours a day).
Say your sort code and account number.
You can then ask your bank for a new debit card.

context:
Naturalisation
Many people have lived in Germany for a long time.
They feel a strong connection to Germany.
That is why they want German citizenship.
You can obtain German citizenship through naturalisation.
Why is naturalisation advantageous?
Naturalisation has many advantages:
You can take part in elections without restriction and thus play an active role in shaping politics.
You have access to all professions without restrictions under immigration law.
You can also become a civil servant.
For example, in the police, as a teacher or as a judge.
You have secure residence for the rest of your life.
You no longer have to obtain permits from the immigration authorities or go to consulates or embassies.
You can work, live or travel anywhere in Germany.
As a German citizen, you also have EU citizenship if you were not a German citizen before.
This means that you are also allowed to stay in all other EU countries without restriction and work, study or live there without authorisation.
You enjoy state protection.
This means that you cannot be deported or extradited to another country.
You also have protection in German embassies abroad if you do not also have citizenship of that country.
What requirements do you have to fulfil?
Naturalisation is subject to a number of conditions:
lawful, habitual residence in Germany for 8 years (note: there are exceptions, e.g. passed integration course, married to a person with German citizenship)
Permanent right of residence
Proficiency in the German language (German B1)
Commitment to the basic democratic order
Livelihood is secured through own gainful employment
No criminal offences committed (petty offences are not an obstacle)
renounce previous citizenship (except for persons with citizenship from the EU or Switzerland)
Knowledge of living conditions in Germany
Knowledge of the legal system and the social order (test "Living in Germany")
You must also submit a declaration.
With this you confirm that you are not pursuing or will not pursue any anti-constitutional endeavours.
This means that you may not pursue any activities that are contrary to the fundamental values of democracy.
This will be checked by the security authorities.
What documents do you need?
Application for naturalisation
Current photograph
Certificate of birth, marriage if applicable, divorce if applicable (for documents in a non-German language: translation by an officially sworn interpreter)
Valid national passport with residence permit
Proof of German language skills (e.g. school report, certificates, completed vocational training)
Proof of "Living in Germany" test
Proof of family income for the last three months
Sometimes the authorities need further documents.
It is therefore best to ask in advance.

Office for Immigration and Integration

Job centre and citizens' income
What does the job centre do?
The job centre looks after people who receive citizen's allowance.
Citizen's allowance is the basic income support for jobseekers.
Jobseekers are supported by the job centre in their search for a job or qualification.
What is the citizen's allowance?
Citizen's income is basic security for jobseekers.
It is a benefit provided by the welfare state.
The citizen's income ensures the minimum subsistence level for people who cannot finance their living expenses from their own income or assets.
The citizen's allowance must be applied for at the job centre.
The citizen's allowance is financed from tax money.
Who receives citizen's allowance?
Citizen's income is paid to people who are capable of work and entitled to benefits.
These are people who...
are at least 15 years old and have not yet reached retirement age.
live in Germany and have their centre of life here.
can work at least 3 hours a day.
are in need of assistance.
Asylum seekers do not receive a citizen's allowance.
They receive benefits in accordance with the Asylum Seekers' Benefits Act.
Recognised refugees receive citizen's allowance.
Which job centre should I contact?
There are many different job centres.
Each job centre is responsible for a specific municipality.

Offers for Children
Deutsch mit Socke
Deutsch mit Socke is a film series that helps children between the ages of 5 and 10 take their first steps in the German language.
In each short video, Esther (a young woman) and Socke (a red sock) talk about all kinds of things – just like in real life.
Socke is red, imaginative, a bit cheeky and full of energy.
This leads to many situations in which Esther and Socke speak and interact in German together.
Children can easily identify with Socke.
The material is also about this: The children should - like Socke - be able to speak and interact in the foreign language.
The videos are accompanied by activities and a student booklet.
Die Bienenretter
With this free app, children from the age of three can learn German in a playful way.
With no previous knowledge of the language, they leave the protection of the forest together with a squirrel and a bear and embark on an exciting journey to save the sick bees.
On their way through the snow-covered mountains where a lynx, the guardian of the medicinal plant, lives, they encounter animals that help them and teach them more than 900 German words.
"Die Bienenretter" can be played on two different levels of difficulty and offers up to six hours of fun.
Vocabulary app for children
Each word is first introduced and then practised with different exercises.
Illustrations and educational games help with this.
Die Sendung mit dem Elefanten
The little blue elephant and his friends offer stories to discover, marvel and laugh along with, for children between the ages of 3 and 6. Each programme lasts about 25 minutes and is also very suitable for language training.
Kid's channel WDR Maus
The page with the mouse (Maus) offers educational programmes – in which, for example, the production or function of an everyday object is explained – as well as audio stories, games or even handicraft tips.
Each "Sendung mit der Maus" presents complex issues in an entertaining and understandable way for children between the ages of 6 and 9 and lasts about 30 minutes.
It is also suitable for language support for children with some previous knowledge.
Lingo für Kids
With Lingo, children between the ages of 8 and 12 can practise German and learn new things.
There are exciting texts for reading and listening, experiments and handicraft tips.

German driving licence
You need a driving licence to be allowed to drive in Germany.
To drive a car on your own, you must be at least 18 years old.
You have to get your driving licence at a driving school.
You have driving lessons there and an exam at the end.
The exam consists of a written part and a practical part (driving).
You have to pay for your driving licence yourself.
Foreign driving licence
You want to drive in Germany and already have a driving licence from your home country?
Then you first have to check whether your driving licence can also be recognised in Germany or whether you also have to pass the practical and/or theoretical driving test again here.
For EU citizens, the foreign driving licence is generally recognised.
Driving licences from third countries such as Syria, Iraq or Afghanistan are usually not recognised in Germany.
You have to take the theoretical and practical exam again.
In addition to German, the theoretical exam can be taken in the following languages: Arabic, Turkish, Spanish, French, Russian, Polish, Romanian, Italian, Portuguese,and English.

After registration and accommodation in the reception centre, you will have to apply for asylum in person.

An interpreter will also come for this appointment.
You will submit your asylum application.
And you will receive important information about the asylum procedure.
Have you submitted your application for asylum?
Then you will receive a residence permit.
This is proof of your legal residence in Germany and your application for asylum.

Government of Swabia
Central Immigration Office Swabia
zab-poststelle@reg-schw.bayern.de
Residence obligation
The residence permit is initially associated with spatial restrictions.
This means that you may only stay in the district of your reception centre.
Would you like to leave the area temporarily within the first three months?
Then you need a permit from the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees.
After the three months, you will need a permit from the relevant immigration authority.
Depending on your country of origin and the course of your asylum procedure, this spatial restriction applies for different lengths of time.

Then you must inform the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees of your new address yourself.

The German higher education system and helpful links
To be able to study in Germany, you need the school-leaving certificate "Abitur" or "Fachabitur".
Usually, you need to speak and write German at level C1 in order to study at university.
You can also start studying in Germany without a university entrance qualification.
However, you must have your university admission from your home country recognised as soon as possible.
Different types of universities
In Germany, there are different types of higher education institutions that lead to different degrees and career paths:
Universities: strongly scientifically oriented;
suitable if you want to do a doctorate (make the doctorate)
Universities of applied science: very practically focused
Universities of art, film and music: The focus is on artistic subjects such as fine arts, drama, illustration, instrumental music or modern media (direction, camerawork, screenwriting etc.)
All higher education institutions offer Bachelor's and Master's degree programmes.
There are both state and private universities.
Most universities in Germany are funded by the state.
Private universities sometimes impose high tuition fees.
University of Augsburg and the Augsburg University of Applied Science
In Augsburg, you can either study at the University (www.uni-augsburg.de), at the University of Applied Sciences (www.hs-augsburg.de/international) or at the private University of Applied Sciences for Economics and Management (FOM) for working people (www.fom.de/hochschulzentren/augsburg) .

context:
Equality between women and men
In purely legal terms, women and men are equal in Germany.
This means that women and men have the same rights in Germany.
Every person - whether man or woman - is allowed to make decisions about themselves and their own lives.
Women and men should have the same opportunities - personally, professionally and within the family.
In everyday life, equality between women and men has not yet been achieved in Germany.
This is why the Federal Government is actively promoting equality.
For example, through these activities:
The compatibility of family and career is promoted through measures such as parental allowance, the expansion of childcare and all-day education and childcare programmes in primary schools.
The federal government is committed to increasing the number of women in management positions.
Women still earn less than men.
In future, men and women should receive the same salary for equivalent work.
The so-called "Remuneration Transparency Act" makes a valuable contribution to this.
The law makes it possible for employees to receive information about the criteria and procedures according to which they are paid.

Integration courses for adults
What is an integration course?
The Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF) offers integration courses.
In an integration course, you will learn German and many things about Germany.
For example on topics such as...
Work and career
Training and further education
Childcare and education
shopping
Housing
Rights and duties in Germany
How can I do an integration course?
When do I have to attend the integration course?
Voluntary attendance: Authorisation certificate required
Would you like to attend the course voluntarily?
Then you needauthorisation from the BAMF, a so-called "certificate of eligibility".
With this authorisation certificate, you can register for an integration course at a language school.
Whether or not you receive a certificate of eligibility depends on your residence status.
You can get help with this from the "Learn German" counselling service.
The counselling service can also help you with the application for the eligibility certificate.
Obligation from the Office for Immigration and Integration
Some people are required to attend an integration course by the Office for Immigration and Integration.
This means that they must attend the integration course.
Important information at a glance
- The general integration course lasts several months and takes place full-time or part-time (e.g. for people in employment).
- It consists of a language course with 600 teaching units (short: UE = 45 minutes) and an orientation course on life in Germany with 100 UE.
- The aim is to reach language level B1 on completion of the course.
You will then receive a certificate.
- The certificate is important.
For example, if you are looking for work or want to do an apprenticeship.
The certificate can also be important if you want to stay in Germany permanently and need a permanent residence permit.
- There are also special integration courses for certain groups of people.
For example, for women (with childcare), working people or people who cannot read and write.
- Participants with a BAMF authorisation certificate pay 220 euros per module (=100 hours).
They can get 50% of this back if they successfully complete the course within two years.
- Participants without a BAMF authorisation certificate pay 440 euros per module (=100 hours).
- The course is free of charge for recipients of social benefits.
They will be exempted from the costs on application.
Necessary travel costs can also be reimbursed.
The language counselling centres offer individual advice on this.

context:
Decision of the BAMF
Decision on the asylum application
After the personal interview, the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees examines all descriptions, information and evidence.
It examines whether one of the four forms of protection exists on the basis of the Asylum Act:
entitlement to asylum
refugee protection
subsidiary protection
prohibition of deportation
The asylum application is only rejected if none of these forms of protection can be recognised.
The decision is justified in writing and sent as a "notification" to
the applicant or persons who have been authorised in this procedure (lawyers).
the competent immigration authority.
The decision is negative
If your asylum application is rejected, you will receive a negative decision and a threat of deportation.
The threat of deportation means that you will be asked to leave the Federal Republic of Germany by a certain date.
If you do not leave by this date, you may be forcibly deported.
There are two different types of refusal:
Simple rejection: you must leave the country within 30 days.
Rejection as "manifestly unfounded": In this case, the deadline for leaving the country is only one week.
Contestation
If you do not agree with the rejection, you can appeal against the decision in both cases.
This must be done very quickly after receiving the decision.
Therefore, go immediately to the integration and refugee counselling centre in your accommodation.
You will receive support there.
You should always seek advice and representation from a lawyer specialising in asylum and residence law if you wish to take legal action.
You will be informed of all deadlines and legal options in the written decision: This information is called "Rechtsbehelfsbelehrung".
Voluntary departure
If you decide to leave voluntarily, you can receive financial support for a new start in your country of origin.
You can get advice on voluntary departure
here :
Central Return Counselling South Bavaria
info@zrb-suedbayern.de
www.zrb-suedbayern.de/
Inform the
Foreigners' Registration Office as soon as possible that you wish to leave the country voluntarily.
The decision is favourable
You are recognised as eligible for protection.
The next steps are:
Fictitious certificate or electronic residence permit (eAT): Immediately after the positive BAMF decision has been delivered, you must obtain an identity document or its equivalent.
You can obtain this from the Office for Immigration and Integration.
You are now authorised to work in Germany without restriction.
If you do not have a job and are dependent on support, you will no longer receive money from the social welfare office.
You must submit an application to the job centre.

context:
Religion
Religion in Germany
Germany is a predominantly Christian country.
Many people belong to the Catholic or Protestant faith.
Of course, there are also many people who belong to other faiths.
Meanwhile, many people no longer have a denomination.
This means that they do not belong to any religious community or denomination.
Christianity still plays a major role in Germany.
That is why there are also many statutory Christian public holidays.
Other religious holidays are also observed at school.
Pupils who wish to celebrate religious holidays can be exempted from school.
This should be discussed with the school at an early stage.
Faith is a private matter in Germany.
State and religion are separate.
However, the state and religion work closely together.
For example, there are religious education lessons at school.
In Germany, every person is free to choose their own faith.
Freedom of religion is a valuable asset.
Freedom of religion
Freedom of religion is the law in Germany.
Everyone has the right to choose and practise their own faith.
The Basic Law must not be violated in the process.
Freedom of religion includes
All people are free to practise and choose their religion and beliefs.
All people have the freedom not to be religious.
Anyone who does not believe in God may say so publicly.
People with different religions and beliefs may marry each other.
A marriage must be performed at the registry office.
Only then is it a legally binding marriage.
Any person may also marry within the framework of religion.
However, this is not legally binding in Germany.
The Basic Law can be read in nine languages(German, Arabic, English, Farsi, French, Kurdish-Kurmanci, Russian, Spanish, Turkish): www.bamf.de (search term: "Broschüre: Das Grundgesetz").

Consultation
Personal interview
This is the most important appointment in the asylum procedure.
You will receive an invitation.
An interpreter will be present.
You must attend this appointment.
Can't make it?
Then let us know as soon as possible!
You need an important reason.
You must provide this.
Otherwise your asylum application may be rejected or the procedure may be discontinued.
Procedure of the interview
At the interview, you can explain why you had to flee your country.
You will be asked questions about
Your biography
Your life situation
Your journey to Germany
the reasons for your persecution in your country of origin
Do you have evidence for your statements?
Then you should bring it with you.
The hearing will be conducted by specialised staff.
Who is allowed to come to the hearing?
You do not have to go to the hearing alone.
You can be accompanied to the hearing by
a lawyer
a representative of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR)
another person of trust who is not involved in an asylum procedure themselves
In the case of unaccompanied minors, the guardian may attend the interview.
Your statements will be translated.
And there is a protocol.
The minutes will then be translated back to you.
So you can add to it or correct it if necessary.
At the end you will receive the minutes.
If everything is correct, you confirm this with your signature.

The Asylum Procedure Law (AsylVfG) and the Asylum Seekers Benefits Act (AsylbLG) generally stipulate that asylum-seekers and persons with exceptional leaves to remain (Geduldete) should live in asylum seeker accommodation facilities.
Some federal states provide accommodation in private homes.
In all federal states, recognised refugees may move into their own home.
In the accommodation and everywhere in Germany there are rest periods from 10 pm in the evening to 6 am in the morning.
The quiet times are also regulated by law.
No loud music is allowed during this timeand everyone should be quieter.
You and your neighbours in the accommodation and in the neighbourhood need the quiet times so that living together works and remains harmonious.
You will find the rest periods and other rules in the "house rules" of your accommodation.
The House Rules are there to regulate life together.
Please adhere to the House Rules and always respect the rules and resting times.
Asylum seekers who, for special reasons, wish to move out of their allocated accommodation and rent a flat themselves must agree on this with the Benefit Authority (Leistungsbehörde) in advance.
30 eurosper person per month are withheld from the benefits paid to the asylum seeker and the electricity is granted as a payment in kind.
Attention should be paid to economical energy consumption and correct waste separation.

Public holidays
No work is done on public holidays for religious or secular reasons.
Shops and authorities are closed on these days.
The following public holidays are on the same date every year:

All Saints' Day
25.12.
1st Christmas Day
26.12.
2nd Christmas Day
Other public holidays change from year to year.
You can find an overview of public holidays in Bavaria here.
School holidays
School holidays are the times of the year when pupils are off school.
In Bavaria, the new school year begins every year in September.
Autumn holidays: There is a week around All Saints' Day (public holiday).
Christmas holidays: There are two weeks around Christmas and New Year (public holidays).
Winter holidays: There is one week of winter holidays in February.
Easter holidays: There are two weeks of holidays in spring
Whitsun holidays: There are two weeks of holidays in early summer.
Summer holidays: In summer, the school year ends at the end of July/beginning of August with six weeks of holidays.
You can find an overview of all upcoming public holidays and school holidays here.
Religious holidays
Jewish, Muslim and Orthodox pupils are exempt from lessons on certain religious holidays: www.km.bayern.de/ministerium/termine/ferientermine.html
Please inform the school if your child cannot come to school due to these holidays.
Intercultural calendar
The intercultural calendar provides an overview of the most important holidays of the different religious communities.
Time change
There is also a time change in Germany.
This means that the clock is moved forward one hour from winter to summer time.
From summer to winter time, the clock is set back by one hour.

Entry - visa procedure
Entry as part of a visa procedure
If you are travelling to Germany on a D visa for a longer stay, you must note the following after your arrival:
Firstly, you must register at your chosen place of residence.
German law stipulates a period of 14 days for this.
In the district of Augsburg, you register at the residents' registration office in your town hall.
Here you will
find a list of all municipalities and town halls in the district.
Once you have registered, you will receive a registration certificate.
The second step is to apply for a residence permit:
The national visa (category D) will be issued to you for entry.
It is not issued for the planned duration of your stay.
You therefore need a residence permit.
You must apply for the residence permit at the immigration office.
It is important that you apply for the residence title while your visa is still valid.
The residence permit is limited in time and can be extended.
Depending on the reason for your entry, the residence permit also regulates
whether you are allowed to work or not,
what work you are allowed to accept and
whether time restrictions apply to employment in Germany.
Extension of the residence permit:
Please note that you should apply to extend your residence permit 6 to 8 weeks before it expires.
Depending on the purpose of your stay, there may be other things to consider.
You can also obtain this information from the Immigration Office.

context:
Public transport
There is a good network of public transport in Augsburg and the surrounding area, such as buses and trams.
The Augsburger Verkehrs- und Tarifverbund (AVV) is responsible for this network.
You can find all the important information on the AVV website at www.avv-augsburg.de.
For app users, both the AVV (app: AVV.mobil) and Stadtwerke Augsburg (app: swa FahrInfo) offer free apps for download.
You need a ticket to travel by bus or tram.
There are often checks on buses and trams.
If you don't have a ticket, you will have to pay a fine.
The second time, you will be reported to the police and fined a much higher amount.
So make sure you always have a valid ticket with you!
Fare zones and price levels
The area covered by the AVV is divided into zones.
The price of the ticket depends on the number of zones travelled through.
The more zones you pass through, the more expensive your ticket is.
Each zone corresponds to a price level.
Each zone is only counted once.
For example, if you travel through zones 20, 10 and 20 again, you need a ticket of price level 2 or 2 stripes on the stripe card.
However, the outward and return journeys count as two different journeys.
The city area of Augsburg comprises fare zones 10 and 20.
The district of Augsburg comprises zones 30 - 70.
You can find the fare zone maphere.
The timetables with the fare zones are also displayed at the stops.
Note: Your ticket is also valid if you change trains.
The most important tickets
You can find detailed information on all tickets and current prices here.
Germany ticket
For 49 euros a month, you can use all local public transport and travel throughout Germany.
The Deutschlandticket is a subscription.
This means that it is automatically renewed every month.
But you can cancel it every month.
Always by the 10th of each month at the latest (for example: 10th March) for the following month.
You can order the Deutschlandticket here.
It will then be played on your smartphone.
You will need the "meinAVV" app for this.
You can find the app in your smartphone's Apple or Google store.
Discount ticket for students, trainees, civil servants or volunteers
In Bavaria, these groups of people can get a discounted Deutschlandticket.
The discount ticket costs 29 euros.
It is also valid nationwide.
The person's place of education or residence must be in Bavaria.
To apply, you need proof of eligibility from your educational institution.
You can apply for the discount tickethere.
Stripe card
9 strips for flexible use (one strip per zone)
Valid for 3 hours (no return and round trips)
No take-away options (one strip per person and zone)
You can find more information about the Streifenkarte here
Single tickets
Single journey from A to B
Valid for 1 hour (no return and round trips)
No take-along options
4 stops after boarding buses or trams, even across zone boundaries
Transfer possible
You can find more information about single tickets here.
Day ticket
Any number of journeys on the selected day
For adults aged 15 and over
For one person or groups (each additional person costs a surcharge)
Up to 4 children under the age of 14 can travel free of charge.
Valid Monday to Friday from 9:00 a.m., Saturday, Sunday and public holidays all day;
valid until closing time (i.e. until the last bus or tram leaves).
Please note: The names of the travellers must be handwritten on the day ticket!
You can find more information about the day ticket here.
365-euro AVV ticket for school pupils, trainees, interns and FSJ volunteers
The 365-euro AVV ticket is available for school pupils, trainees, interns and young people doing a voluntary social year.
For €1 a day, you can travel as often as you like on trams, buses and trains throughout the AVV network area - around the clock!
You can pay for the ticket in instalments or all at once.
You can find all the information here.
Monthly travelcard for school pupils
Pupils do not have to pay for bus and tram travel themselves.
They can submit an application.
The costs for the monthly travelcard will then be covered.
For this, the journey to school must be more than 2 kilometres for pupils in grades 1 to 4. For children and young people from year 5 onwards, the journey to school must be longer than 3 kilometres.
Further information and download of applications: www.landkreis-augsburg.de
Collective call taxi (AST), on-call bus
The call-and-collect taxi (AST for short) and the on-call bus operate when there are no regular bus or train connections.
A taxi picks you up from the station or a bus stop, for example, and takes you to the door of your desired destination.
The journey must be requested by telephone at least 30 minutes before departure.
The regular AVV prices apply.
You can find more informationhere.
AktiVVO - minibus on demand
The minibus runs on demand without fixed stops and without a fixed timetable.
The minibus journeys can be booked by telephone or in the "AktiVVO" app.
Passengers can hop on and off at one of the AktiVVo stops or the AVV regional bus stops within a short space of time.
The fare for the AktiVVo corresponds to the regular AVV fares.
The AktiVVO minibus commutes in these regions:
Holzwinkel and Altenmünster, Roth- and Zusamtal
Bobingen, Königsbrunn and Schwabmünchen
The AktiVVO only operates in these regions.
It also does not travel to Augsburg.
It does not travel to any places outside these regions.
Augsburg City Zone
In the city of Augsburg, you can use the bus and tram free of charge at a total of 9 stations around Königsplatz and the main railway station.
The free stops are one stop in each direction from Königsplatz and Moritzplatz.
You can find more information here.
At night
With the night bus you are also mobile at night (0.30 to 4 am).
The night buses run from Thursday to Sunday and on public holidays.
Passengers require a special night ticket (also available on the buses).
Regional trains run on some routes.
The regular AVV fare applies here.

context:
Forms of protection in the asylum procedure
Forms of protection in the asylum procedure
Many people are persecuted in their home country.
People can receive protection in Germany.
To do so, you must apply for asylum.
By applying for asylum, you start an asylum procedure.
It decides whether you are allowed to stay in Germany.
There are different forms of protection under German law.
This is because there are different forms of persecution.
In the asylum procedure, your situation is analysed in detail.
You will then be granted a form of protection.
You can find an overview of the forms of protection here.
Under the links you will find information in German, English, Turkish, Russian, French and Arabic.
Entitlement to asylum
Politically persecuted people are granted asylum in Germany.
This is stated in the Basic Law (Art.
16 A).
You receive protection status if you are persecuted by the state in your home country because of
Your ethnicity
Your nationality
Your political convictions
your religion or
your membership of a particular social group (e.g. because of your sexual orientation).
Some people also fear punishment if they return to their home country.
This form of protection also applies in this case.
Find out more
Refugee protection
The Geneva Refugee Convention has defined who is considered a refugee.
The definition says: A refugee is outside the country of origin.
He or she is persecuted by a state or non-state because of one of the following characteristics
ethnicity
religion
nationality
political conviction
membership of a particular social group (e.g. due to sexual orientation)
Legal basis: Section 3 para.
of the Asylum Act (AsylG)
Learn more
Subsidiary protection
Subsidiary protection applies to people who are at risk of serious harm in their country of origin.
Or who cannot claim protection in their country of origin.
The threat can come from a governmental or non-governmental source.
These include
Death penalty
torture
inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment
serious individual threat to the life or integrity of a civilian due to indiscriminate violence in an international or internal armed conflict
Legal basis: Section 4 (1) AsylG
Learn more
National ban on deportation
A person seeking protection may not be deported if
the return would constitute a violation of the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (ECHR) or

context:
Important rights and duties when doing an internship
Internship contract:
You do not have to have an internship contract.
It is a good idea to have an internship contract, however.
This is because it specifies the rules of the internship.
Hours of work:
Depending on your age, there are different regulations about working hours during an internship:
For children and adolescents under the age of 15, it is forbidden to work, generally.
Examples of exceptions include work experience for school pupils or, from the age of 13, easy tasks, such as delivering newspapers or providing private tutoring.
For adolescents below the age of 15, there is special protection: They are only allowed to work for 7 hours per day, and for no more than 35 hours per week.
For teenagers between 15 and 18 years of age, the rule is: They are only allowed to work for 8 hours per day, and for no more than 40 hours per week.
For interns who are older than 18, standard working hours of 8 hours per day apply.
However, standard means: It does not always have to be the case.
If there is lots to do, interns are allowed to work for more than 8 hours.
It is not allowed to work for more than 10 hours per day.
Breaks:
Interns can, and must, have breaks too.
For interns below the age of 18, the rule is: For working hours of between 4.5 and 6 hours, interns must have a break of 30 minutes.
For more than 6 working hours, it has to be 60 minutes.
Interns who are older than 18 must have a break of 30 minutes if their working hours exceed 6 hours.
For working hours of more than 9 hours, it has to be 45 minutes.
Confidentiality:
During an internship, interns learn a lot about how a business or a company is run.
Much of this information is confidential.
In other words: Interns are not allowed to mention any of this information to anyone.
This is known as “Schweigepflicht” (confidentiality).
For example:
Somebody might be doing an internship at a doctor’s surgery.
There, they will learn a lot about the patients.
The patients’ names and the illnesses they have, for example.
They are not allowed to mention any of this information to anyone.
Illness:
If an intern falls ill, the business providing the internship must be told straight away.
Interns often need a medical certificate from their doctor.
Interns should ask the company they are doing the internship with whether they need a medical certificate.
Days off:
During a compulsory internship, interns have no entitlement to days off.
During a voluntary internship, it is possible to have days off.
This only applies to internships which last for longer than 4 weeks.
The number of days off depends on the age of the intern and the length of the internship.
Behaviour in the workplace:
Hosting interns involves a lot of time and work for the host business.
Interns ought to be aware of this.
They should behave accordingly.
You can find tips on this under “Ten tips for interns”.
Entitlement to an internship certificate
Interns have a right to a Praktikumszeugnis (internship certificate).
In other words: The company or business must provide an internship certificate.
The internship certificate is important for the intern.
It will help when applying for an apprenticeship or work later on.

Family reunification
Marriage and family are under special protection in Germany.
This is why certain people can bring their family members abroad to Germany.
These people usually need a visa to do so.
Therefore, contact the foreigners authority and seek advice.
Which people are allowed to bring family members to Germany?
People with German citizenship
Persons residing in Germany who are foreign nationals with a
settlement permit
Permanent residence permit - EU
residence permit
EU Blue Card
ICT card
Mobile ICT card
Family reunification is excluded for the following groups of persons:
Persons with tolerated stay
Asylum seekers in the ongoing asylum procedure
Persons with temporary residence status
Which family members can be brought to Germany?
Wife and husband
Partner from a registered civil partnership
own underage children
Other family members can only be brought to Germany in exceptional cases of hardship.
The requirements are very high.
These include, for example: uncles, aunts, grandparents, grandchildren.
Unaccompanied refugee minors can be joined by their parents.
This applies up to the age of 18.
What requirements must be met?
In principle, the following applies:
The purpose of family reunification is to bring the family together.
The aim is therefore to form a family or partnership.
Spouses must be at least 18 years old.
The marriage or registered civil partnership must have already existed in the country of origin.
All other requirements vary depending on the group of people.
It will be checked whether the requirements are met.
You will need to submit various documents.
It is best to seek advice from the migration counselling service or the foreigners authority .
Simplified family reunification for persons with protection status
Have you been granted protection status in an asylum procedure?
And you would like to bring family members to join you?
Then simplified family reunification applies.
This means that some requirements are waived.
What do you have to do?
You must submit the application for family reunification within three months of being recognised.
Did you miss the deadline?
Then a discretionary decision applies.
This means that the authorities will make a decision based on certain criteria.
Further information on family reunification for persons with protection status can be found on the website of the Federal Foreign Office in German, English and Arabic.

The German healthcare system
There are many institutions in Germany that are part of the healthcare system.
The healthcare system comprises three different areas:
Outpatient medical care by doctors and pharmacies ("outpatient" means: patient goes home after care)
Inpatient medical care through acute care in hospitals ("inpatient" means: patient stays in hospital for treatment)
Health protection of the population through offers of the public health department, e.g. infection protection and preventive offers ("preventive" means: offers to maintain health and not to get sick)
Outpatient and inpatient care provide medical treatment for sick people.
Every person can decide for himself to which doctor or medical institution they would like to go (freedom of choice).
The public health department ("Öffentlicher Gesundheitsdienst") fulfils many different tasks.
You can find a list here.
The health office also fulfils preventive tasks (for example: information and counselling on health).
The aim is to ensure that all citizens in the district enjoy a healthy life.
For example, numerous projects are organised in schools.
These projects take a playful look at the topic of “health”, thus raising awareness of the importance of healthy living.
You can find more information about the health department at www.landkreis-augsburg.de/gesundheitsamt.
You can find health promotion and prevention offers in the district of Augsburg and informative articles here.

context:
Important information on internships
What is an internship?
An internship is a temporary position.
In other words: Interns work for a business for a limited period of time.
An internship can be done in almost every profession.
An internship helps you to…
... get to know a new profession,
... get to know a work environment in practice,
... and / or deepen theoretical knowledge through practical (professional) experience.
What are the advantages of an internship?
Doing an internship before embarking on your career can be very helpful.
Interns become familiar with professions and areas of work.
They learn which career is the right one for them.
Interns get to know companies and businesses.
They find out whether of not they wish to work there.
Interns establish contacts which may be useful when they first embark on their careers.
The company or business gets to know the intern.
After the internship, this can end up turning into a paid position or an apprenticeship.
Who benefits from doing an internship?
An internship can be beneficial to anyone.
For example, employers consider interns when employing new staff.
Internships are particularly useful to:
Pupils,
students,
those who are embarking on their careers (to gain professional experience),
those who wish to change their careers,
people who have been out of work for some time.
The most important kinds of internships
Compulsory internship:
Internship for school pupils:
At school, pupils often have to do a work placement.
An internship for school pupils often takes just one or two weeks.
The idea is for school pupils to get an idea of what working life is like and get some initial ideas about what direction their careers should take.
Internships whilst at university:
In order to graduate, it is often necessary to do an internship.
The schedule and duration are usually determined by academic regulations.
The compulsory internships allow students to acquire their first professional experience.
Voluntary internship:
Anyone can do a voluntary internship – whether a school pupil, a student or an adult.
The intern and the company or business determine the duration of the internship together.
Payment
During their internships, interns are sometimes paid.
But not always.
This depends on many factors.
For example, the type of internship, the duration, and the sector.
Interns have a right to be paid if
the internship lasts for more than three months
and it is voluntary.
This regulation does not apply to compulsory internships which take place in the context of academic studies.
The rule also does not apply to trainees under the age of 18.

Dublin procedure
The Dublin procedure covers the 28 EU member states as well as Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Switzerland.
The Dublin procedure determines which country is responsible for carrying out your asylum procedure.
As a rule, it is the country in which you were registered for the first time.
This is done with an electronic data comparison.
It is possible that Germany is not responsible for carrying out your asylum procedure.
If Germany is not responsible, you will be sent back to the country responsible for you.
If you do not agree with this decision, you can seek counselling.
You can seek professional legal advice on whether it makes sense to lodge a complaint with the administrative court.

A district is an amalgamation of several towns, markets or municipalities.
The district of Augsburg comprises a total of 46 towns, markets and municipalities.

The district of Augsburg is an attractive place to live and work.
That is why more and more people are moving to the district.

The district of Augsburg is very popular with companies, investors and start-ups.
For example because of

its proximity to the city of Augsburg
ideal transport connections.

City or countryside?
The district of Augsburg surrounds the city of Augsburg from the north, west and south.
Nevertheless, the city of Augsburg and the district of Augsburg are two independent municipalities.
The city and district of Augsburg work closely together in many areas.

context:
Legal proceedings
Legal proceedings
You do not agree with the negative decision on your asylum application by the BAMF?
Then you can take legal action.
You are the "plaintiff" or the "claimant".
The BAMF is the "defendant".
If you take legal action, the Administrative Court in Munich will review the BAMF's decision.
If it agrees with the BAMF, the action will be dismissed.
The obligation to leave the country remains in place.
If the administrative court does not agree with the BAMF, you will receive a residence permit.
The BAMF is then obliged to grant you protection.
You can also appeal against a favourable decision by the BAMF.
For example, if you do not agree with the form of protection recognised (exception: recognition of refugee status).
In any case, you should seek advice and representation from a lawyer specialising in asylum and residence law.

What is the Skilled Labour Immigration Act?
Skilled workers can immigrate to Germany more easily.
This applies to skilled workers with
vocational training lasting at least two years or a university degree.
a university degree.
The Skilled Labour Immigration Act sets out the rules.
You can find out more here.
Criteria for skilled workers
The following three criteria are generally considered:
1) Qualification
With the EU Blue Card, skilled workers with a recognised qualification can come to Germany.
2) Experience
People with professional experience may come to Germany.
This applies to people who...
have acquired a recognised professional qualification abroad and
can prove at least 2 years of professional experience.
A salary threshold applies to these people.
This means that they must earn more money than the specified minimum amount.
People without a professional qualification recognised abroad must have their professional qualification recognised in Germany.
3) Potential
People without a concrete job offer can also work in Germany.
The opportunity card was introduced for them.
It is based on a points system.
These criteria are taken into account:
Qualifications
German and English language skills
work experience
Relevance to Germany
Age
Potential of spouses and partners
An important innovation for asylum seekers
Are you an asylum seeker?
Then you can apply for a residence permit as a skilled worker.
You do not have to leave the country.
And you do not have to go through a visa procedure.
You must withdraw your application for asylum.
That's what you need:
a recognised qualification
a job offer or an existing employment relationship

Important information on pregnancy and birth
Pregnant women are under special protection in Germany.
They are entitled to counselling and medical care.
Guide "Maternal health"
The "MaternalHealthGuide" provides answers to many specific questions.
It is available in seven languages:
English
Kurdish
